speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Mr. T. G. W. Ashbourne (Grand Falls-White Bay):
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO METHOD OF MARKETING NEWFOUNDLAND SALTED COD
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) I should like to address a question to his parliamentary assistant. Is the Minister of Fisheries able to inform the house whether the government has made any decision as to the method of marketing Newfoundland salted cod fish at the end of the five-year period established in the terms of union?

speakeroldname: Mr. J. Waison MacNaughl (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO METHOD OF MARKETING NEWFOUNDLAND SALTED COD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay was good enough to give advance notice of this question.
In the terms of union the government of Canada agreed to continue for a five-year period the organized marketing system for the export of salted fish. That system, operated by the Newfoundland fisheries board, grants an exclusive export licence to a group known as the Newfoundland Associated Fish Exporters Limited, known as NAFEL.
The government has taken note of the views of the Newfoundland fishermen and merchants that some plan of organized marketing is necessary. Newfoundland salt fish production is among the world's largest and carries therefore its own selling problems. Certain of the large markets have single buying agencies that make a single selling agency in Newfoundland desirable. Dollar shortages in the main markets add to the difficulties. To try, therefore, to revert to independent merchant selling next year would be to court the danger of market disruption-a danger that would affect the

Inquiries of the Ministry maritime and Quebec salt fish trades as well as Newfoundland. Some system of organized marketing for Newfoundland is necessary.
The existing system of merchandising through NAFEL has provoked certain criticisms from fishermen and others. To take account of their criticisms, the federal government proposes to make certain modifications to the present system.
1.	Since the fishermen's organizations are not represented on NAFEL or its directorate, the Newfoundland fisheries board is being instructed to establish by July 1, 1953, a consultative committee on salt fish marketing. This committee will make continuous review of NAFEL's operations in the marketing of salted fish, the state of the markets, relative prices, costs, and other associated matters. This committee is to be convened by the fisheries board and to include fishermen's representatives, representatives of NAFEL, and a representative from the provincial government of Newfoundland. At these meetings the fisheries board has been instructed to see that a full revelation of facts on marketing is made to the committee.
2.	The government intends to continue the powers of the Newfoundland fisheries board with respect to the marketing of salted fish for a further three-year period as from March 1, 1954.
3.	The exclusive export privileges of NAFEL will be modified by changes in its agreement with the Newfoundland fisheries board.
The most important of these will be a broadening of the opportunities for interprovincial trading. The Newfoundland fisheries board will be prepared to permit sales of wet salted and pickled fish between Newfoundland exporters, including fishermen or groups of fishermen, and buyers from the mainland and continental U.S.A. To protect the Newfoundland fishermen, however, these buyers should make prearranged sales with such Newfoundland exporters in the form of contracts and these contracts shall be arranged before April 30 each year. Copies of contracts are to be deposited with the Newfoundland fisheries board, which will issue the export permits during the season. These transactions may be arranged between buyers and sellers without the intervention of NAFEL and will, therefore, be free of any levy by NAFEL. This provision for prearranged sales should minimize the possibility of fishermen putting up more wet salted or pickled fish than the markets can absorb.
If mainland buyers do not make such forward contracts and if they wish merely to make spot purchases of Newfoundland fish,

either wet or dried during the year, they may do so through NAFEL as at present.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
The house in committee on Bill No. 225, to amend the Excise Tax Act-Mr. Abbott- Mr. Robinson in the chair.
On section 11.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I understand that the committee was considering clause 12.
No, clause 11.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall clause 11 carry?

No. Just before the committee rose last evening I was drawing to its attention the terms of the note on clause 11 which, after explaining that the excise tax on radios was being separated from the excise tax on television sets, winds up with this sentence:
The Item has been further clarified by using more descriptive terms.
I said last night that my understanding was that that was a considerable understatement because according to my information this section in fact extends the operation of the act. That is my information. If it does, then it is in effect and in fact a section whereby money is being raised or, in other words, a money bill. The parliamentary-assistant shakes his head when I say that the effect is extended. I therefore ask very definitely whether it is not extended at least to the extent of bringing within its purview the articles on which an appeal was made to the tariff board and concerning which the tariff board said that they were not covered. The phraseology in question is "telecast receiving units". I am proceeding on the assumption and on the belief that this section does extend taxation, and that it is therefore a money bill. I am pointing out, Mr. Chairman, that it is not supported by any resolution. I go further on that basis, Mr. Chairman, and I point out that it is improperly before the committee because, if


it is in fact a money bill, and if in fact it is raising money, it should have been preceded by a resolution, and that is not the case.
Therefore, following that, I wish to ask whether in fact on February 19 notices were sent to the relevant officials advising them that the additional materials brought under the act would from that day on be subject to tax. I would like to have that question answered first, if I may.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I respectfully differ with the opinion of the hon. member for Greenwood. I have to express the opinion, which is the opinion of the law officers of the crown, that the tubes, sets and apparatus to which my hon. friend has referred are subject to tax under section 6 as it was, and as it can be read on the page of the bill opposite section 11. The apparatus is described as radio broadcast, telecast and music receiving sets. The installations are mostly in private homes. The sets are imported completely manufactured and include some seventeen tubes in addition to the cathode ray television tube and the loud speaker. The value, duty free, is around $216.
Now, let us look at what the old section says:
Phonographs, record playing devices, radio broadcast or telecast receiving sets or tubes therefor, apparatus for receiving radio broadcast and music . . .
The opinion of the law officers of the crown has been and is that all the apparatus, the sets and tubes which I have mentioned as being included in these rediffusion sets, are covered by section 6 as it was; and that the new words of subsection (b) of new section 6 are only for clarification purposes. The law officers do not agree with the decision of the tariff board. A tax has been levied in the past. There was an appeal to the tariff board which was granted for these rediffusion sets as they apply to television but yesterday a request for leave for appeal was heard by a justice of the exchequer court who has reserved his judgment. The legal position now, at the time I am speaking, is that in the opinion of the law officers of the crown the new wording does not extend the taxation, it only clarifies the section.

I find that very hard to understand, but let me ask this definite question. Does the parliamentary assistant agree that the tariff board did reach a conclusion that certain of the articles now covered by this wording on which taxation had been collected were not properly taxable? Is that a fact?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is not a final decision; it is being appealed from.
Does the decision not take effect from the time it is made?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Not if there is an appeal.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Perhaps I can relieve my hon. friend's doubts about the legality of the matter. Conceding, for the purpose of argument, that it does extend the tax, if he will look at the terms of the resolution upon which this bill is before the house he will see that it reads, resolved:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Excise Tax Act-
And I pause there.
-and to provide, amongst other things: and it enumerates a number of things.
The opinion of the law officers is and has been for some time that it is quite sufficient, in order to comply with the provisions of the British North America Act, that the resolution should be merely in the terms "resolved that it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Excise Tax Act". That justifies any amendment that it may be desirable on the part of the crown to introduce. As a matter of practice it has been usual to enumerate in the resolution the principal changes; but I am pointing out to my hon. friend that even if this provision did extend the ambit of the section, which, as my parliamentary assistant has indicated, we do not believe, the resolution preceding the introduction of this bill is quite sufficient in law to justify such action.
Do I understand the minister to say that the general words of the section to which he has referred would authorize an increase in taxation to any limit?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Quite. To any limit at all.

That is a
new idea to me.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It happens to be true.
I am taking the minister's word but may we have an opinion from the law officers? I would be interested to hear what they would say.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If my hon. friend would take the trouble to see the law clerk of the house he would reassure him of that very quickly.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there has
been quite a lengthy discussion on tires and tubes for replacement purposes on farm trailers. At page 3114 of Hansard for March 19, for instance, the hon. member for Huron North said:
There is going to be some difficulty about this. The tires for a trailer or any farm machine are not suitable for speeding on the highway. They just cannot be used on a car because if you used them at any speed you would wear off the tread in a few moments. There is a great difference between a tire used for farm work and one used on the highway.
My answer at that time was:
I will say again what I said this afternoon, that according to the proposed amendment the test of the exemption would not be on the tires and tubes themselves; it would be on the vehicles on which the tires and tubes are to be used. Following the representations made by my hon. friends this afternoon, I said that speedy consideration would be given to the possibility of applying the test to the tires and tubes.
Consideration has been given and the officers of the Department of National Revenue have been in touch with the representatives of the manufacturers of tires and tubes to discover whether it is possible to have a test on the make of the tires and tubes used on farm machinery. It has been possible to find a wording which, I believe, will cover the situation. If my hon. friends will look at section 12 as it reads now I will tell them the purpose of the amendment which I will ask the Minister of National Revenue to move. The intention of the amendment is to make three exceptions in line 36 after the word "therein". We will there make a special paragraph which will be numbered (i) which will read as follows: When used exclusively for the original equipment of such self-propelled machines, automotive vehicles, trailers or other wheeled attachments,
Then, (ii) reads:
When used exclusively for replacement purposes on machinery designed for and used only for farm purposes.
Then, the addition is in (iii), which reads: When designed and catalogued for farm machinery and used on farm trailers used exclusively for farm purposes.
I believe that covers exactly the problem that was raised by hon. members. May I repeat the important words:
When designed and catalogued for farm machinery and used on farm trailers used exclusively for farm purposes.
May I add it appears from the discussions the officers of the Department of National Revenue have had with the manufacturers of tires and tubes that there are no tires and tubes which are made especially

Excise Tax Act
for trailers. The situation is that tires are made for farm machinery, and those tires are bought by some farmers for use on their trailers. I see that the hon. member for Battle River is nodding his head, so he approves of my statement of the position. I believe he is one of those who have made representations in order to obtain such an amendment.
That is the point I was going to make. It is clear, then, that tires and tubes for farm trailers will be sold without the tax?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: When designed and catalogued for farm machinery; that is what was requested.
As I understand it, then, replacement tires for farm trailers, to be used exclusively on the farm, if it is an implement tire, is tax free?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is exactly the position.

May I ask a question there? There are some farmers who have one farm in one end of the township and another farm at the other end of the township. They would have to go on the highway and pull that trailer, perhaps with a tractor, from one farm to the other. Would that still be considered used exclusively on the farm?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
May I repeat the wording, which I believe will satisfy my hon. friend? It says:
When designed and catalogued tor farm machinery and used on farm trailers used exclusively for farm purposes.
It does not say it has to be used only on the farm, but exclusively for farm purposes.
If that farmer put the trailer behind his car and drove to town, perhaps with a load of grain, would it still be considered a farm trailer?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It is still used for farm purposes, so it is still a farm trailer. But if he travels long distances at a high speed with this type of tire, it will cost him a lot of money.
He will have a blowout.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
I move:
That section 12 of the bill be deleted, and the following substituted therefor:
12. Section 13 of schedule I to the said act is repealed and the following substituted therefor:
"13. Tires and tubes:-
(a) Tires in whole or in part of rubber for self-propelled machines or automotive vehicles of all kinds, including trailers or other wheeled attachments used in connection with any of the said machines or vehicles . . , fifteen per cent;

(b) Inner tubes for use in any such tires . . . fifteen per cent;
the tax on the articles enumerated in paragraph (a) and (b) of this section does not apply to the goods mentioned therein
(i)	when used exclusively for the original equipment of such self-propelled machines, automotive vehicles, trailers or other wheeled attachments,
(ii)	when used exclusively for replacement purposes on machinery designed for and used only for farm purposes, or
(iii)	when designed and catalogued for farm machinery and used on farm trailers used exclusively for farm purposes."

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The committee has heard the amendment. Is it the pleasure of the committee to adopt the amendment?

speakerposition: stagedirection

Section as amended agreed to.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: May I propose that we take the schedule page by page?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
If that is agreed to, and since I am in an agreeable mood, perhaps I might be permitted, as a matter of privilege and without entering into an argument, to place upon the record the fact that I, for one, cannot agree with the statement made by the Minister of Finance a moment ago when he was replying to the hon. member for Greenwood as to the terms of a resolution preceding a bill imposing taxes. As I say, no point of order has been raised and no point of order has to be settled. I do not think it would be fair, however, to those of us on this side of the house for that statement to be left on the record without any suggestion that there is an argument on the other side. I should like to place on the record the fact that citation 515 of Beauchesne's third edition reads as follows:
Debate and amendment on the stages of the finance bill or other bills imposing taxes are governed by the ordinary rules of relevancy and, if any of the provisions of the bill should be found to go beyond the resolutions of the committee of ways and means or other committee of the whole house, as agreed to by the house on report upon which the bill is founded, a further resolution must be passed by the committee of ways and means or other committee of the whole house, and agreed to by the house before those provisions are considered in committee on the bill, or the bill must be amended so as to conform to the resolutions to which the house has agreed. Amendments to the bill which are not covered by resolutions of the committee of ways and means or other committee of the whole house are out of order. Amendments have also been ruled out of order as not relating to the finance of the year.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: What date is that?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: It is from page 185 of Beauchesne's third edition.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: What date is that?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: It is taken from May, and it is an old principle that was laid down quite a few years ago.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I understand that the minister said the legal opinion of the law clerks is now that-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I am surprised to hear my hon. friend, who is a lawyer, deprecating an opinion because it is an old one.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is not what I said. I said it was an old citation. My friend knows that even courts have reversed their own previous judgments and opinions.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: It was not my purpose to get into an argument over the matter.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I just want the record to be straight.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
That is what I want. I have great respect for the opinions of the law officers and law clerks, but after all it is their function to advise us and the practice is determined by parliament. I submit that up to this time parliament has made no change in this practice which calls for a resolution setting out what is coming to precede all bills that impose taxation.
Now, as I said before the interruption of a moment ago, it was not my purpose at this point to enter into an argument over this question because I think it can be contended that the particular matter we were debating today is referred to in the resolution, at least in a general way. I do feel, however, that the general rule which the Minister of Finance sought to lay down should not go unchallenged. In my view it is still a requirement of this parliament that a bill imposing taxation should be preceded by a resolution setting out the terms of that proposed taxation.

Perhaps I might be allowed to say one word. When the Minister of Finance made this statement, the strength of which surprised me-I respect him, both as a lawyer and in his capacity as a minister-I asked that I be furnished with the opinion of the law officers of the crown. While it was not clear whether I was to have it in writing, I do hope that I may have it in writing. In any event, there was a strong statement made by the minister which I found very surprising, but which I nevertheless took, but I am asking that I may be fully satisfied as to the authority upon which he made it.
Who said the law officers of the crown were infallible, anyway?

Who are they, anyway?

No. Last night when I rose in this chamber and attempted to make a few brief remarks on clause 1 of the bill now before the committee, I was informed by the parliamentary assistant that my remarks should come under section 13; and the chairman at the time asked me whether I was satisfied to defer my remarks until section 13 came before the committee. Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of order. The hon. member is now referring to matters which should come under section 13. As a matter of fact, following-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole

For the sake of brevity, Mr. Chairman, I shall bow to your ruling. Thank you.

I do appreciate the fact that my hon. friend mentioned the matter on the floor of the house and that the fisheries council of Canada were kind enough to take the matter up collectively with the department; and we all appreciate the way in which it was dealt with by the minister and by the officials of his department. These concessions may seem small but they are appreciated by all the fishermen in the 
maritime provinces; and I believe the fishermen down there realize that the members from there are all working toward the same end.

Is that prepared from cream, or is it a vegetable oil preparation?

Mr. Chairman, I am sure we should commend the parliamentary assistant for the manner in which he is supplying the information required today. I believe it is under this part of the bill that I might be permitted to make some observations concerning one of my constituents in Hastings South. I speak about the W. T. Hawkins Company Limited, who manufacture a product known as caramel corn snacks.
The department is familiar with this subject, because for the last two years the plight of this company has been brought to its attention, as well as to that of the minister. Although we have been received very sympathetically, unfortunately something more than sympathy is needed and desired. It is all right to sympathize with a man who is drowning, but it is much better to throw him a rope.
I am sure the parliamentary assistant is familiar with this particular case, so I shall not be long in placing the situation before the committee. Perhaps it would be sufficient to point out that caramel corn snacks is a product manufactured in Tweed. It is made from popcorn, with some sugar added, admittedly. However, I do feel that it should fall into that class described as "cereal breakfast foods not including beverages".
This is a corn product. At the present time it is required to pay a 15 per cent excise tax, while from 90 to 95 per cent of all competitive corn products, such as cheese-coated, powdered and salted popcorn sold in Canada is not covered by the excise tax.
Caramel corn snacks is sold in direct competition with these other types of popcorn. There are, of course, the cereal products

known as sugar crisp, sugar puffs and com pops, manufactured by Post, Quaker Oats and Kellogg, which are advertised, sold and consumed as sweet snacks, but without paying any sales tax or excise tax.
I suggest the department should take another look at this situation, because the company is now suffering from receding returns, inasmuch as it is meeting with sales resistance, due to the excise tax. Their sales have fallen so low that the government would be collecting practically no excise or sales tax. If they were permitted to operate as their competition operates-that is, without the restraint of this 15 per cent excise tax- their sales would increase, they would pay more sales tax, and would also be subject to income tax.
As I have pointed out, they say they have now reached the point where there is a diminishing return to the department. If these so-called cereal products are sold not only free of excise tax but also free of sales tax, it would seem that the department is not using all in the same way. I think all hon. members in the committee would agree that the government has never tried to place a business in a position where it could not operate. They have always endeavoured to be helpful and I think in this instance the government would do well to amend the regulations and exempt popcorn. I am appealing on behalf of this company which is situated in the village of Tweed. This is a small village without a great many industries and the W. T. Hawkins Company has been giving considerable employment.
As 95 per cent of popcorn products are now outside the act as far as excise taxes are concerned, I think the government might very well permit this company to market their products tax free. Could the parliamentary assistant inform the committee whether this could be done? I see no reason why it could not.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The candied popcorn to which my hon. friend has referred competes with candy and not with cereal breakfast foods which have been mentioned.
It competes with popcorn, which does not pay anything.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: This is candied popcorn which competes with candy. As a matter of fact, there is a decision of the tariff board that it is a substitute for candy and taxable as such 15 per cent excise tax and 10 per cent sales tax. subsubtopic: RESPECTING TERRITORIAL COUNCIL, ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think we should have from the minister some explanation as to the effect of this bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Resources and Development
subsubtopic: RESPECTING TERRITORIAL COUNCIL, ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE, ETC.
speechtext:
I shall be glad to give that, Mr. Speaker. The main purpose of this bill is to revise and consolidate the Yukon Act. The act is now contained in chapter 215 of the Revised Statutes of Canada and in four amending acts passed in the years 1940, 1941, 1948 and 1951.
Hon. members will recall that in the last amending act provision was made for increasing the number of the members of the council from three to five by establishing two new electoral districts in the Whitehorse area. This change is now effective. The election of the members of the new council took place last summer and the first meeting of the enlarged council was held in October. It will be recalled that the elected council has legislative authority but that it does not have executive authority.
The Yukon Act was first passed in 1898. The last revision was in 1927. With the continued and healthy growth of the territory, especially within the last decade, it is desirable that the act should now be revised. The
[The Deputy Chairman.]
legislative powers conferred upon the commissioner in council by the present act are in most respects similar to those conferred upon provincial legislatures. There are, however, several subjects over which the provinces have jurisdiction and with respect to which it is now proposed to confer jurisdiction upon the commissionex in council. These are roads, wills, the property of married women, coroners and inquests, controverted elections, the establishment and maintenance of hospitals, and agriculture. At the present time all these matters are within the jurisdiction of parliament, and cannot be legislated upon by the commissioner in council. It is proposed to drop from the act the sections relating to them, and appropriate ordinances will be enacted by the Yukon council.
There are in the present act a number of sections relating to criminal matters. Appropriate equivalent sections will be contained in the new Criminal Code. These are therefore no longer necessary in the Yukon Act and authority is being sought to drop them.
The bill would confer jurisdiction upon the commissioner in council to make ordinances for the borrowing of money by the commissioner for the purpose of meeting the annual expenditures pending the receipt of territorial revenues. For example, difficulty has been experienced in financing the yearly bulk purchases of liquor stocks. This will be overcome if power is given to the commissioner to borrow the necessary funds for such purpose. Again, the bill seeks to give the commissioner in council the right to pass ordinances authorizing the commissioner to borrow money for the purpose of making loans to municipalities for the construction of municipal works, and to authorize him to make such loans. It is proposed, however, that no money shall be borrowed or lent without the approval of the governor in council.
Authority is also being sought to give the commissioner the right to hold land for the beneficial use of the territory. As hon. members know, all crown lands in the territory are under the administration of the federal government and are in the name of the crown in the right of Canada. In carrying on the government of the territory it is necessary for the commissioner to hold or acquire land for territorial purposes, such as property required for public buildings, schools, hospitals and other works. At present no such authority exists.
Another section of the bill would confer upon the governor in council the power to make regulations concerning reindeer. They are the property of the federal government and therefore are not within the legislative

powers of the commissioner in council. While all the herds of reindeer are now located in the Northwest Territories, it may be that in the future it will be expedient to move some of them into the Yukon. In such an event regulations will be required to provide for their control and management.
In recent years a number of interesting archaeological discoveries have been made in the Yukon and no doubt there will be many more in the years to come. It is desirable that the sites should be preserved, and the bill therefore seeks authority to give the governor in council the right to pass regulations for this purpose.
There are several other minor amendments which members will note as the various sections are reviewed by the committee of the whole. I might add, however, that in carrying out the revision of the act we have attempted to have it follow the pattern of the new Northwest Territories Act which was enacted at the last session of parliament. The bill before us contains 54 sections. Of these only 14 either are new or embody substantial changes from the present act. The remaining 40 sections are intended chiefly to effect the consolidation. They embody no substantial change from the provisions of the present act.
The present act with amendments to date contains 132 sections. Seventy-four sections are being dropped. As mentioned, the sections refer to criminal law, married women's property, wills, coroners and jurors and other miscellaneous subjects.
The Yukon Territory is an area rich in natural resources. Prospecting is active and interesting discoveries are being made. It also has one of the most fascinating histories of any part of Canada and it seems important to provide the type of legislation which will encourage its growth and development and at the same time protect the reminders of its colourful past.
Hon. members who have noted the number of times they have been invited in recent years to amend legislation affecting our north country will I am sure regard this bill as a further indication of the government's interest on behalf of the people of Canada in this vast and increasingly important area.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I wish to direct a question to the minister purely from the point of view of obtaining some information in connection with the bill itself. I am not advocating that procedure because I am not in a position to do so; I do not know the situation well enough. But I am wondering what the disadvantages are, both with respect to the Yukon and the Northwest Territories, from the standpoint of incorporation as a province and generally what the governing factors are in this question as to a territory becoming a province. speakerposition: Minister of Resources and Development
subsubtopic: RESPECTING TERRITORIAL COUNCIL, ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE, ETC.
speechtext:
The population of the Yukon territory, as revealed by the 1951 census, was 9,096. Of this total approximately 1,500 were natives. The governing factor as to whether or not these territories should be considered on a basis of provincial status is whether or not they can afford normal provincial services. Both the Yukon Territory and the Northwest Territories are vast in extent but contain a relatively small number of people, and a relatively smaller proportionate revenue is derived from normal sources.
They simply cannot finance the type of services the other provinces have come to expect. I believe the only way they can be

Yukon Act
financed adequately for the time being is by all the people of Canada through the federal government.

subsubtopic: RESPECTING TERRITORIAL COUNCIL, ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE, ETC.
speechtext: I think that answers the inquiry. I had the idea that the population of the Yukon was greater than that; otherwise I would not have asked the question. What is the population of the Northwest Territories?

speakerposition: Minister of Resources and Development
subsubtopic: RESPECTING TERRITORIAL COUNCIL, ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE, ETC.
speechtext: It is of the order of 10,000, speaking from memory.

subsubtopic: RESPECTING TERRITORIAL COUNCIL, ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE, ETC.
speechtext:
Having spent three very happy years in the Yukon as a young man I am delighted to see that the progress of that part of Canada has justified the bringing in of this new legislation. I am certain it will be of great benefit to the Yukon. Undoubtedly that area has progressed a long way since the trail of '98.
Perhaps the determining factor in the future development of the Yukon will be water power, rather than gold. Does this legislation give full control over water power within the Yukon to the council or to the minister? I am convinced that water power is the essence of the future development of the Yukon.

speakerposition: Minister of Resources and Development
subsubtopic: RESPECTING TERRITORIAL COUNCIL, ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE, ETC.
speechtext: No change is contemplated in the control over water power. The authority rests in the parliament of Canada to make regulations respecting water power in the Yukon and Northwest Territories.

subsubtopic: RESPECTING TERRITORIAL COUNCIL, ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE, ETC.
speechtext: What is the area of the Yukon Territory? I notice that the schedule sets out dimensions, description and location, but not the area.

speakerposition: Minister of Resources and Development
subsubtopic: RESPECTING TERRITORIAL COUNCIL, ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE, ETC.
speechtext: The land area of the Yukon Territory is 207,076 square miles.

subsubtopic: RESPECTING TERRITORIAL COUNCIL, ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE, ETC.
speechtext: What are the names of the commissioners?

speakerposition: Minister of Resources and Development
subsubtopic: RESPECTING TERRITORIAL COUNCIL, ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE, ETC.
speechtext: The commissioner of the Yukon Territory is Mr. Brown. There are five elected members of the council, as follows: Carmacks, Mr. A. R. Hayes; Mayo, Mr. A. Berry; Dawson, Mr. V. C. Mellor; Whitehorse East, Mr. J. L. Phelps; Whitehorse West, Mr. F. D. Locke.

subsubtopic: RESPECTING TERRITORIAL COUNCIL, ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE, ETC.
speechtext: What connection has Major General Young with the Yukon administration?

speakerposition: Minister of Resources and Development
subsubtopic: RESPECTING TERRITORIAL COUNCIL, ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE, ETC.
speechtext:
Major General Young is deputy minister of the Department of Resources and Development. Under the Yukon Act the administration of the Yukon is by instructions given the commissioner from time to time by the governor in council or the minister. Through that connection the deputy minister of the department is in 
constant touch with the administration of the Yukon Territory.

subsubtopic: RESPECTING TERRITORIAL COUNCIL, ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE, ETC.
speechtext:
Who has the
responsibility and authority in connection with areas in that territory containing gold and other minerals? Are those areas administered by the commissioner and members of the council, or by the department here in Ottawa?

speakerposition: Minister of Resources and Development
subsubtopic: RESPECTING TERRITORIAL COUNCIL, ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE, ETC.
speechtext: Gold mining comes under the Yukon Quartz Mining Act, a federal statute. Placer mining of gold comes under another federal statute, the Yukon Placer Mining Act. Other mining operations come under the Territorial Lands Act, a federal statute having application in the Northwest Territories and in the Yukon.

speechtext:

subsubtopic: RESPECTING TERRITORIAL COUNCIL, ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE, ETC.
speechtext: What revenues are collected within the territories that are available to the commissioner and members of the council? What additional funds are required and authorized by parliament, and assigned to the commissioner and his associates, to carry out their responsibilities?

speakerposition: Minister of Resources and Development
subsubtopic: RESPECTING TERRITORIAL COUNCIL, ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE, ETC.
speechtext: In 1951, the last year for which I have statistics, revenues amounted to $1,848,000, while total federal expenditures were $5,626,000.

subsubtopic: RESPECTING TERRITORIAL COUNCIL, ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE, ETC.
speechtext: I understand that the $1,848,000 was raised by the commissioner and his council within the territory, and that that amount was available for expenditure by them. Then there was a further appropriation by this parliament amounting to around $4 million. For what purpose was it used?

speakerposition: Minister of Resources and Development
subsubtopic: RESPECTING TERRITORIAL COUNCIL, ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE, ETC.
speechtext: It is used for the normal provincial expenditures on highways and the like. Highway costs are very high, in relation to the number of people using them and the vast area covered. There has been an extensive program of highway construction, including the great highway from Whitehorse to Mayo. We are now trying to extend that from Stewart Crossing, near Mayo, to Dawson city. Then there are further expenditures for welfare, education, and all those other items found in the provinces.

subsubtopic: RESPECTING TERRITORIAL COUNCIL, ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE, ETC.
speechtext: Would the minister give the expenditures under the headings of highways, education, and any others there may be, through which the $5 million is used?

speakerposition: Minister of Resources and Development
subsubtopic: RESPECTING TERRITORIAL COUNCIL, ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE, ETC.
speechtext:
For the fiscal year 1952, for example, the expenditures on the Yukon council were $11,875; for territorial offices,

$56,569; education, $177,224; public works, $39,447; health and public welfare, $238,476; municipal administration, $79,374; game and publicity, $18,270; general and unforeseen, $10,051; department of roads and bridges, $484,025.

speechtext: Where is the present seat of government for the territory?

subsubtopic: RESPECTING TERRITORIAL COUNCIL, ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE, ETC.

subsubtopic: RESPECTING TERRITORIAL COUNCIL, ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE, ETC.
speechtext: Is there any reason to expect that it may be changed from time to time?

speakerposition: Minister of Resources and Development
subsubtopic: RESPECTING TERRITORIAL COUNCIL, ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE, ETC.
speechtext: There may be reason to change the seat of government, although I would not say it might be necessary from time to time. As hon. members know, for many years the seat of government was at Dawson, which was the centre of activities following the gold rush of 1898. At one time Dawson was one of the largest cities in Canada. Its population has receded until there are now only a few hundred people. On the other hand Whitehorse has grown markedly in population. Being on the Alaska highway it is the centre of communication and much more accessible. The administration of the Yukon can be carried out much more expeditiously, efficiently and economically from Whitehorse than from Dawson. Several years ago it was decided to move the administrative headquarters from Dawson to Whitehorse, and that move was made recently.

He is supposed to be a man especially selected by the governor in council and should be the ablest man of the lot because of his special qualifications. Probably he would come from outside the territory. The other men are going to be elected by popular ballot and they may benefit from some person of experience to help -them and make suggestions.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subsubtopic: RESPECTING TERRITORIAL COUNCIL, ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE, ETC.
speechtext:
Don't you believe in
democracy?

subsubtopic: RESPECTING TERRITORIAL COUNCIL, ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE, ETC.
speechtext: Certainly I believe in democracy, but I believe also in precedent. Here we have a council of five members, and then in the next section provision is being made for a Speaker. A majority of the council would be three members who, including the Speaker, would constitute a quorum. I think it is worth considering having the commissioner preside at council meetings.

speakerposition: Minister of Resources and Development
subsubtopic: RESPECTING TERRITORIAL COUNCIL, ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE, ETC.
speechtext: We have considered that and decided that the best operations would result if the commissioner did not sit in with the council. Perhaps the main difference between this council and the one that acted in Newfoundland is that in this instance it has no executive authority, its authority being legislative only.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subsubtopic: RESPECTING TERRITORIAL COUNCIL, ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE, ETC.
speechtext: How does the Speaker get appointed? I have looked at the act and can find no reference to the Speaker in the definitions or anywhere else.

speakerposition: Minister of Resources and Development
subsubtopic: RESPECTING TERRITORIAL COUNCIL, ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE, ETC.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subsubtopic: RESPECTING TERRITORIAL COUNCIL, ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE, ETC.
speechtext: Should not there be some provision for that? It just seems as though he is picked out of thin air.

subsubtopic: RESPECTING TERRITORIAL COUNCIL, ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE, ETC.

minister power under the act to issue general instructions as to procedure in connection with such things as the election of the

Speaker? I think it would be wise to have something of that kind.

speakerposition: Minister of Resources and Development
subsubtopic: RESPECTING TERRITORIAL COUNCIL, ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE, ETC.
speechtext: I suppose under the general authority given to the minister that could be done, but we have left it to the council to conduct its own business and to devise ways of doing so. That has been found to be satisfactory. Leaving to the council the right to select a chairman or, as we call it here, a Speaker, has worked satisfactorily. There has been no question about it so far and I am sure there will not be.

subsubtopic: RESPECTING TERRITORIAL COUNCIL, ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE, ETC.
speechtext: Would the minister take another look at this section to see whether there should not be something added before the word "Speaker"? I am somewhat impressed by the suggestion of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. I am simply trying to be helpful. It may be there should be something that has just been left out.

speakerposition: Minister of Resources and Development
subsubtopic: RESPECTING TERRITORIAL COUNCIL, ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE, ETC.
speechtext: I shall be glad to do that. There is no change from the existing act in that respect, but I do not believe the hon. member for Peel would wish the legislation held up on that account. I will look into that.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subsubtopic: RESPECTING TERRITORIAL COUNCIL, ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE, ETC.
speechtext: Has the minister the other act there? I see that the explanatory note on the opposite page says there is no change in substance. Has the minister the actual wording of the previous section 16?

subsubtopic: RESPECTING TERRITORIAL COUNCIL, ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE, ETC.

A majority of the council, including the Speaker, shall form a quorum.

subsubtopic: RESPECTING TERRITORIAL COUNCIL, ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE, ETC.
speechtext: Might I suggest that there might be a subsection 3 added to clause 9 which would read something like this, that the person obtaining the largest majority should be the Speaker, or that the council shall have the power to elect a chairman or Speaker.

subsubtopic: RESPECTING TERRITORIAL COUNCIL, ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE, ETC.
speechtext: The word "Speaker" in section 13 is not the most appropriate term that could be used for a council of this size. The word "Speaker" is used for the officer presiding over a parliament or other body having the functions of a parliament. In this case I think the term "chairman" would be much more appropriate both with respect to the functions which the council has to discharge and the number of members on the council. A chairman chosen from one of their number would be much more fitting, so far as the term is concerned, than "Speaker".

On section 14-Governor in council may prescribe the qualifications of electors, candidates, etc.

subsubtopic: RESPECTING TERRITORIAL COUNCIL, ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE, ETC.
speechtext:
This clause seems to grant very exceptional powers. I should like the minister to explain why they are necessary. The clause reads in part as follows:
-the commissioner in council may prescribe the qualifications of those entitled to vote at an election of members of the council and of those eligible for nomination and election as members of the council and the reasons for or matters by which an elected member may be or become disqualified from being or sitting as a member of the council.
Under our system of government it would seem to me that very autocratic powers are being granted to the commissioner in council.
I should like the minister to explain why they are necessary and why the bill could not set out the qualifications required. I should like to know why this power should be left to the commissioner and his associates.

speakerposition: Minister of Resources and Development
subsubtopic: RESPECTING TERRITORIAL COUNCIL, ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE, ETC.
speechtext:
Hon. members will recall that when the Northwest Territories bill went through the same question was raised. It was considered at that time that if we were going to have what is in effect a local legislature they should have responsibility for and authority over those things that normally fall within the jurisdiction of a local legislature to the greatest extent possible. The qualifications of voters is one of them. The existing legislation reads as follows:
The commissioner in council may prescribe the qualifications of those entitled to vote at an election of members to the council . . .
And so on. We are seeking no powers that were not there before, nor are we seeking any powers that do not normally fall within the jurisdiction of a provincial legislature, or in fact a legislature of this kind which is an elected legislature for these purposes.

speechtext:

subsubtopic: RESPECTING TERRITORIAL COUNCIL, ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE, ETC.
speechtext: I see that fees up to $50 per day are being provided for the remuneration of the members of the council. Under these circumstances that would seem to me to be a rather excessive allowance. I think most members would agree that if the commissioners have to travel any distance they should be reimbursed for their out of pocket expenses, but it would appear to me that $50 a day is excessive.

speakerposition: Minister of Resources and Development
subsubtopic: RESPECTING TERRITORIAL COUNCIL, ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE, ETC.

subsubtopic: RESPECTING TERRITORIAL COUNCIL, ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE, ETC.
speechtext:
Has the minister received any representations as to the ability or inability of the people in the territory to raise sufficient funds for educational purposes? How is secondary education handled, or is there any such thing as secondary education in the territory? Has the minister had any representations as to any difficulties experienced by the residents of the territories in providing adequate educational facilities?

Yukon Act

subsubtopic: RESPECTING TERRITORIAL COUNCIL, ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE, ETC.

subsubtopic: RESPECTING TERRITORIAL COUNCIL, ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE, ETC.
speechtext: Including the capital costs?

speakerposition: Minister of Resources and Development

subsubtopic: RESPECTING TERRITORIAL COUNCIL, ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE, ETC.
speechtext: May I ask if there are combined Indian and white schools in the Yukon on the same basis as there are in British Columbia.

speechtext: Perhaps I might seek to answer the question asked a moment ago by my colleague the hon. member for Vancouver East, and to which the minister did not seem to know the answer. subsubtopic: RESPECTING TERRITORIAL COUNCIL, ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE, ETC.

speechtext: May I ask the minister if he can tell us what the present situation is with respect to the manufacture, compounding or importing into the Yukon Territory of intoxicants. I note that according to this provision, which is more or less the same as it was previously, intoxicants are not allowed into the territory except by permission of the commissioner. I gather that this is not a question that is left to the decision of the territorial council but rather it is a decision made by the commissioner, which in effect means that decisions in this matter are made here in Ottawa. speakerposition: Minister of Resources and Development
subsubtopic: RESPECTING TERRITORIAL COUNCIL, ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE, ETC.
speechtext:
As hon. members may remember, two years ago, I think, there was a change made in the Yukon Act to enable intoxicating liquors to be manufactured in the Yukon Territory under the authority of the commissioner in council. That was intended to bring the authority into line with that prevailing in all other provinces in Canada and in the Northwest Territories. It has been decided that for administrative purposes it would be very difficult to summon the council to deal with instances should they occur. It is quite different from the situation here, where it is easy to assemble the council. For this reason

it was found administratively desirable to delegate the authority to the commissioner.

speakerposition: Minister of Resources and Development
subtopic: ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES FOR CONSERVATION PURPOSES
speechtext:
Perhaps I should say a few words about the purpose of this bill, Mr. Speaker. While the bill itself is relatively short, I believe it is of great importance to Canada. Its effects can be both far-reaching and long-lasting.
The conservation of natural resources within the provinces is primarily a provincial responsibility, and there is no desire or intention on the part of the federal government to invade that jurisdiction. The bill is drafted accordingly. Its basic purpose is to enable the federal government to assist provincial governments in carrying out measures of a major character designed to conserve their water resources, and at the same time reduce the hazard of serious flooding.
The interest of the government of Canada in conservation has found expression in the past in a number of important measures which were designed to assist the provinces in respect to special projects of major importance, or to assist them in problems of such wide scope that the finding of a solution was in the national interest. Included among these measures have been the Canada Forestry Act, the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, the Maritime Marshland Rehabilitation Act, the Eastern Rocky Mountain Forest Conservation Act, and the National Parks Act. The results that have been achieved through these acts are well known. I believe all hon. members will agree that Canada has benefited substantially through their operation, and that these benefits will continue to increase as time passes.
We have heard many excellent addresses in this house in the past few years on various

Water Resources
phases of the vast field of conservation. In almost every case it was the expressed wish that more might be done to ensure the conservation of Canada's resources for the continuing benefit of the present and future citizens of our country. It has been pointed out many times that the interests of conservation are quite often opposed to the immediate interests of financial gain, and that too often our resources have been sacrificed for profit.
We all know of many examples where human neglect or lack of knowledge or faulty practices have in the past resulted in forested land being laid waste and farm land turned to desert. We have seen torrents of water pouring down the river valleys from areas denuded of vegetation, to wreak destruction in the cities and towns below. We have seen, too, the dried-up stream beds in heat of summer and urban populations spending large sums in search for adequate water supplies.
Public consciousness of the need for conservation, and of the inherent dangers that lie in faulty practices in the conservation field, has grown with the years. I am sure it is safe to say that the people of Canada are now more conservation-minded than at at any time in our history. The realization of the problem on the part of every citizen is, I believe, the most important factor in achieving the ultimate goal where our renewable resources will be managed in such a manner that they will be, as nearly as possible, available in perpetuity. We have come a long way already from the early days when our resources were looked upon as inexhaustible. This progress has been made through the efforts of public-spirited and farsighted men in all walks of life, in private industry and at every level of government.
The bill which is before us today for consideration is intended as a further step toward conserving our resources, and toward alleviating the damages that have already been suffered. The bill seeks authority for the government of Canada to grant financial assistance to provincial governments for the construction of major water conservation projects. Assistance of the nature contemplated has already been given by Canada through special votes of parliament to various projects which were outside the scope of existing conservation acts. These projects, which included the Luther marsh and Shand dams in the Grand river watershed in Ontario, and the Fanshawe dam on the Thames river north of London, were considered to be of sufficient importance that federal participation was warranted.
[Mr. Winters.!	,
Subject to funds being voted by parliament, we have also informed the government of Ontario that the federal government would assist financially in the construction of a conservation dam on the Conestogo river. My contacts with the government of Ontario on these water conservation measures have been with the minister of planning and development. In each of these special cases a formula has been used whereby the local municipalities affected agreed to pay 25 per cent of the cost, and the provincial and federal governments undertook to pay 37J per cent each; in other words, to share the remaining 75 per cent on a dollar for dollar basis.
The bill now before the house is intended to place this type of assistance on a statutory basis, and thus make it available to all provincial governments. The bill provides for federal contributions up to 37J per cent of the cost of major water conservation projects, with the remaining portion of the cost being borne by the provincial government concerned or jointly by the provincial government and the local municipalities affected. The bill also provides, however, that the contribution of the federal government shall not be greater than that of the provincial government.
This approach to the problem is designed to leave the prime responsibility with the provinces, to whom it has been assigned by the British North America Act, and yet provide sufficient assistance to encourage the undertaking of necessary projects which might not otherwise be carried out. The limitation to projects which are, in the opinion of the governor in council, of a major character will ensure that the taxpayers of all of Canada will participate only in those projects which are of sufficient importance to be of national concern, and which the province could not reasonably be expected to carry out alone.
Hon. members will notice that the bill envisages an agreement in respect to each project, and it is proposed that this agreement shall be between the government of Canada and the government of the province. The bill recognizes, however, that local authorities may be set up within the provinces to deal with particular conservation areas or problems. In fact a number of local authorities have already been established under provincial jurisdiction. These local authorities may actually undertake the work on behalf of their provincial goverhments, and in many cases share in the cost. In these instances there will in all probability be subsidiary agreements between the provincial governments and the municipalities or local authorities covering the terms of their participation.

However, this is a matter for provincial governments and their municipalities to decide.
Sir Clifford Sifton, who is recognized as having been one of Canada's greatest authorities on conservation, pointed out that artificial works can only supplement the place of nature in the regulation of stream flow. While the immediate works envisaged under the terms of this bill will be dams to regulate flow and lessen the danger of disastrous flash floods, it is fully recognized that the construction of dams alone will neither prevent floods nor achieve adequate conservation of the water resources of an area. The restoration of forest cover and other conservation measures in the drainage areas of the rivers are normally required. We have stressed these broader features in all our dealings to date with provincial governments. A most important feature of the Canada water conservation assistance bill, therefore, is the provision for the undertaking by the provinces of ancillary conservation measures in conjunction with projects receiving federal assistance. These ancillary measures will be carried out in all cases except where it is determined by careful study, to the mutual satisfaction of both the federal and provincial governments, that they are not required.
The importance of this provision cannot be overemphasized. It will ensure that any project to which federal assistance may be given will be a component part of an integrated conservation plan for the area in which the project is located. This provision will serve also to encourage the development of broad plans to embrace many fields of conservation in a given area.
I would like to point out that this bill and the Canada Forestry Act will, in effect, be complementary to each other in many instances. When a province wishes to undertake the construction of a water conservation project, and submits a detailed plan of the proposed over-all conservation measures in the area concerned, this plan will be studied with a view to assistance being given under the Canada Forestry Act with respect to reforestation, as well as under the provisions of the bill now before us. Where the ancillary conservation measures include reforestation, that work may be eligible for assistance under the terms of the Canada Forestry Act. In this way, the Canada water conservation assistance bill would also give encouragement to the provinces in the use of the Canada Forestry Act. Hon. members will note that the two main points of programs envisaged by this legislation have to do with water and forest cover, and that both are within the scope of the Department of Resources 68108-2231
Water Resources
and Development through its engineering and water resources branch and its forestry branch. No addition to present staff is envisaged because of this bill.
I wish to stress once again that this proposed legislation is purely enabling in character, and that it does not seek to establish any change in jurisdiction or responsibility. The government of Canada would grant financial assistance under this legislation only after a formal request had been received from the province concerned. The federal government will have no proprietary interest in any of the works to which it contributes.
We have before us legislation which would for the first time offer broad federal assistance to the provinces on a definite basis for the conservation of their water resources. If approved by parliament it will help to round out a really worth-while and comprehensive program aimed at the conservation of Canada's natural resources. As I mentioned earlier, Canadians in all walks of life are becoming daily more conscious of conservation. We already have examples of successful projects that have been undertaken in the water resources conservation field in a similar manner to that provided for by this bill. I feel that these practical examples give evidence that the time has now been reached when federal assistance on a statutory basis can be extended with the firm expectancy that great return to Canada as a whole will be received from the investment.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words in connection with this bill, although when I see the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) looking at me I feel that it is almost sinful to speak at this time.
I must congratulate the minister, first of all, on his statement and his clear C.C.F. analysis of what private enterprise has done in some cases to the natural resources of this country. This group certainly supports this bill as a further step forward in the development of what we hope will finally be an over-all conservation policy for Canada, and we are pleased indeed that the bill provides for ancillary conservation, the relation of the conservation of water resources with the conservation of forest resources and so on. But, Mr. Speaker, my main reason for rising at this time is to say that we are disappointed to know that the provisions of this bill do not include a clause to provide for river bank protection from damage as the result of erosion on navigable rivers.
I mention this matter because this question of erosion or damage from erosion is an extremely serious one to many parts of the constituency I represent, and is of increasing

Water Resources
concern to an increasing number of people. It is of concern to the corporation of the city of Trail where, as will be remembered, in 1948 a serious disaster was just averted by prompt action on the part of citizens, the union and the company. It was a co-operative effort to prevent something that might have been extremely serious indeed to that city and to other communities along the Columbia river and the Arrow lakes. But while that disaster at that time was averted, that threat still exists because the federal, provincial and municipal authorities have failed to accept their responsibilities to do something about it.
There are also, in the Creston area of my constituency, a considerable number of farmers who suffer damage from erosion to the banks of the Kootenay river. As a matter of fact there are some 17.3 miles of the banks of the Kootenay river within my constituency. Year after year these farmers suffer considerable damage and are threatened with serious damage, again as a result of no action being taken on the part of the federal and provincial governments to devise a policy to meet that threat and that situation. It is a constant problem to these people; it is a constant expense; and to the people farming reclaimed land it represents a constant danger.
The farmers of whom I am speaking have reclaimed some 15,000 acres of bottom land that was producing no wealth whatever a few years ago. As a result of the initiative of these people in that community and in surrounding districts, those 15,000 acres of land have been brought into production and are producing a great deal of wealth in the form of grain, forage and other crops, and provide a considerable amount of fodder for a number of cattle. This production has brought prosperity to the district, and has provided a considerable sum in additional taxes to the federal and provincial coffers. Yet nothing is done about this problem which is such a serious one to many of my constituents on the Columbia and the Kootenay rivers.
I am constantly receiving letters about the matter. I just want to quote briefly from a letter I received from a gentleman who has been prominent in reclamation work in Creston throughout the years and who speaks for those who are greatly concerned about the constant waste and loss occasioned by the erosion caused by the floods on the Kootenay river.
I might say, Mr. Speaker, that I was looking up some of the government reports in this connection, and there is no question about it that on the banks of navigable rivers the
[Air. Herridge.l
federal government is recognized as the riparian owner and has some legal responsibility, as well as a moral responsibility. This gentleman, Mr. Guy Constable, whom a great many people throughout British Columbia know and whom I am sure the officials of the department will know quite well, wrote me a two-page letter quite recently about this situation, and I am going to quote two short paragraphs. He says:
Certainly a national policy embracing water and soil must straighten out the ownership of water as between the dominion and the provinces and the responsibility for river erosion which is becoming every year more serious, and that brings me to the purpose of this letter primarily.
He goes on to deal with the problem of river erosion. Then he goes on to deal with a situation which they face at the present time and the present policy of local people as a result of that erosion. In this paragraph of his letter he says:
The present policy is and has been up to now, to draw back the dikes and reconstruct them further away from the river. It is a losing policy in every way, almost one of despair, wasteful of land and effort, and of money since it is not a corrective. I think it parallels the situation I have described as to irrigation. Reclamation of wet lands is a national benefit, and the land cannot bear the whole cost when adjacent to navigable waterways.
I find, Mr. Speaker, that not only does that situation exist in the constituency which I have the honour to represent, but it is one that we find in many places in Canada. I have been reading what literature I could get in this connection in recent months, and I happened to have in my hands recently the report of the select committee on conservation, 1950, for Ontario. I note that this problem is dealt with at some length in this booklet and I am going to quote one short paragraph, because I think it states our argument in this group which is that the federal government should accept responsibility for initiating a policy that will overcome, as a result of federal, provincial and, in some cases, municipal co-operation, the damage caused by erosion. I now quote from page 114 of this report of the select committee on conservation:
This problem, it should be noted, is not unique in this province. It is world-wide. European countries, particularly Denmark, the Netherlands and England, have been fighting erosion from the seas for centuries. It is a most pressing problem on the American shores of lakes Ontario, Erie and Michigan, and along the entire lengths of the Atlantic and the Pacific coasts.
The problem reached such proportions that the government of the United States set up within the war department, in the office of the chief of engineers of the United States army, a beach erosion board which has been carrying on research and giving leadership in the combating of shore erosion in that country.

Losses through shore erosion have today reached a point where they can no longer be considered the responsibility of the individual person whose land is affected, but rather, because of the federal government's control of navigable waters, a problem to be considered jointly by the dominion and provincial governments and the municipality concerned. This committee therefore recommends that:
The dominion, provincial and municipal government's should recognize the public responsibility for assistance in lakeshore erosion prevention.
We in this group say amen to those conclusions. No effective action has been taken in any country until a governing body with sufficient influence and financial resources has taken the lead to do something about the erosion situation. This is a long-term problem in Canada, an increasing problem; and once again I say that we in this group regret very much that there is no provision in the bill for at least a start on the part of the government on this most important problem, a very serious one to Canadians in various parts of Canada.
It is a long-time problem, but no action has been taken to date. It is time something was done. If the minister does not see fit to introduce an amendment to the bill that would remedy the situation, we would urge his department to give consideration to the problem as it exists in Canada from the Atlantic to the Pacific, with a view to taking steps to improve the situation in the very near future.
