Mr. Speaker, I had not intended speaking at length in this debate, but as one who has been interested for years in conservation I believe I should take this opportunity to say a word in commendation of what the Minister of Resources and Development (Mr. Winters) has done in bringing this bill before the house.
Although he is one of the younger members of the government, I wish to congratulate him upon his vision and foresight, and upon his ability to gather from his observations and studies the importance of things people in Canada are thinking, and feeling should be done, and especially at this time I would commend him for bringing a bill of this kind before the house with a view to making statutory some of the arrangements that had been made hitherto only by agreement between the federal and provincial governments. Let me commend him and congratulate him warmly and sincerely for what he is doing.
We may not agree that the bill is everything we would want, but I am always happy to see a start made. I do not look upon this start as encompassing the whole scope of what will be encompassed eventually in legislation of this kind. Doubtless changes will be made, and in all likelihood as the years and sessions go by members will bring to the minister's attention changes that should be made in the act to enlarge its scope.
I am happy that, through the action he is taking today, the minister is giving leadership in the field of conservation. That is important. The last time I spoke on this subject I believe I said leadership ought to come from a senior government in Canada. That leadership is now coming from the point from which it should come, and this gives me considerable satisfaction.
I do not look upon this legislation as being exclusively Social Credit legislation in any respect; nor do I think the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) has any logical basis for saying that it is C.C.F.

Water Resources
legislation. Yet I was interested in what the hon. member did say about the exploitation of our natural resources by private enterprise. We hear that so constantly from socialist members; that private enterprise has done this, that private enterprise has been responsible for that, or has been responsible for not doing the other thing.
In other words, at every opportunity that presents itself they try to undermine private enterprise. Let me point out that if any of the resources of this country have been exploited wrongfully by private enterprise, and if there has been wastage or destruction in that exploitation, it has not been the fault of private enterprise so much as that of the government that has allowed it to take place.
Governments in the various provinces are presumed to own and control the resources for and on behalf of the people. If adverse exploitation has taken place in any of the provinces it has been because of a lack of watchfulness and good management by government. That ought to be stressed. It is because of wrong policies on the part of governments that these things have happened. No one can say that it is private enterprise and because private enterprise is faulty in its concept of what should be done.
I want to say that I believe in private enterprise. I believe that we should take every action possible to preserve private enterprise as being the best possible means of getting the finest results in any of our activities, and to manage and build up our economy. I wanted to say that much because when we hear these repetitions about the failings and weaknesses of private enterprise it sort of gives me a sick feeling at my midriff.
As the minister gains experience in administering this bill and dealing with the provinces I hope he will find it possible to enlarge the scope of the legislation to include something along the line mentioned by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge), that is the prevention of erosion. We suffer from erosion, not only of river banks but generally throughout large areas. I think sometimes we overlook the fact that erosion of land occurs over such a wide area that the province concerned, or at least some provinces, might not have the resources to cope with it. No doubt in some cases they would have to come to the senior government for help.
That principle has been recognized to a considerable extent in connection with irrigation schemes to prevent further damage by erosion. However, I am quite sure that soil erosion is caused by other things than wind

and water. I am expressing the hope that in the years ahead the minister will find it possible to enter into agreements with certain provincial governments to provide assistance in putting a stop to widespread causes of erosion which the provinces cannot handle themselves. I shall end by saying that I think the minister has made an excellent start, and I commend him for it.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. J. Browne (St. John's West):
subtopic: ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES FOR CONSERVATION PURPOSES
speechtext:
When this matter was first announced in the speech from the throne I made a study of water conservation. It seems to me that this bill is putting into general effect what has been the policy in connection with Ontario. Several projects costing millions of dollars have been carried out in this province. I do not know if similar projects have been carried out in other provinces.
I was wondering hoyv far the minister had thought out this thing and whether this legislation will be available to all the provinces. On reading the report of the Department of Resources and Development I noticed that very little has been done in my province, and I suppose I can be excused for making special reference to that. There are no large municipalities in that province outside of St. John's and perhaps Corner Brook where measures of conservation such as are envisaged by this bill would be required. The province would have to bear almost two-thirds of the cost of any project of this kind.
Will this legislation provide assistance in power development? I notice that the section which enables the minister to make agreements with the provinces refers to the building of dams for the conservation of water and I should like to know if that could be extended to include power projects where a river might be diverted to flow into other rivers so that a profitable power project could be brought into being.
This bill is something new, and it seems to indicate that the federal government has a great deal more money than the provinces. While some of these projects may be of great benefit, nevertheless they are local in character and cannot be regarded as being national. The entry of the dominion government into this field will give them a certain control over matters which otherwise would be exclusively provincial. I think everyone will agree that it is desirable that we should get the best results from potential water power sites in all parts of Canada. The provinces naturally are most interested in doing something along these lines, but the fact is that this amounts to a subsidy to the provinces in order that they may use that power to the best advantage.

I notice that the same section which gives the minister the power to make agreements also stipulates certain conditions in regard to reforestation. That brings me to something which was mentioned by the hon. member for Kootenay West. The hon. member was blaming private enterprise for the conditions which exist today in many provinces where natural resources have been depleted.
I think in the past governments were not sufficiently aware of the speed with which natural resources could be depleted. The passage of time has brought to the attention of all persons and governments the desirability of adopting measures to protect our natural resources. I think it can be said that the private paper companies have shown special interest in introducing the most advanced practices in fire control. I think they have done more along these lines than the governments because their whole operation depends upon the availability of forest resources.
In Newfoundland they have worked things out in such a way that the forest resources will be available in cycles. They will cut an area today and it will grow again so that in 25, 30 or perhaps more years the company can come around and cut that area again. In the meantime they will be cutting in other places. They are doing that in the Anglo-Newfoundland Development Company's operations around Grand Falls, where a paper mill was established in 1904.
There is great value in flood control from the point of view of the tourist industry. I have mentioned this before, and I know that hon. members who come from provinces where there are salmon rivers realize that rivers are becoming depleted of fish because of a lack of regularity in the water flow whereby the salmon are prevented from having ready access to the headwaters of the rivers. If there is not sufficient flood control a river will dry up in the summer and the salmon cannot enter. If there are no salmon there will be no tourists visiting that particular section.
I assume that if this bill is going to have its full effect a provision will be incorporated in the agreements so that sort of thing can be done. Provinces could erect dams to regulate the flow of water in salmon rivers to enable the salmon to ascend regularly and thus provide more sport. There is no doubt about it that the salmon rivers are more valuable to the province as a sporting attraction than merely for the spawning of salmon for commercial fishermen. They bring more revenue.

The question is what are the qualifications before an application would be eligible for assistance under this bill. In the first place the project must be of such size and importance as to merit federal government participation on behalf of all the taxpayers of Canada. It must be the size of project that would not normally be undertaken by the provincial and municipal governments alone. It must be a project designed to conserve water and, in order to be of the nature of projects already carried out, have as one of its main purposes the prevention, or at any rate the minimizing, of serious flash floods. My hon. friend is thoroughly familiar with the Shand and Luther dams and the proposed Glen Allan dam on the Conestogo river. I can think of no better examples of the type of project that is contemplated than those.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES FOR CONSERVATION PURPOSES
speechtext: Can the minister say to what extent such grants will be authorized? In other words, how much is the federal government prepared to grant toward the over-all picture? Is there any limit?

speakerposition: Minister of Resources and Development
subtopic: ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES FOR CONSERVATION PURPOSES
speechtext: Each project will be considered on its merits. There is no limitation or specification as to the over-all amount involved.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES FOR CONSERVATION PURPOSES
speechtext: Have any requests been received from provinces other than Ontario up to the present time?

speakerposition: Minister of Resources and Development
subtopic: ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES FOR CONSERVATION PURPOSES
speechtext: No specific requests have been received. Requests of a general nature have been received.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES FOR CONSERVATION PURPOSES
speechtext: I should like the minister to answer the question I asked him a while ago. Would the rebuilding of mill ponds and dams in the province of Prince Edward Island be too small a proposition to take into consideration? The local government has already taken on two or three such projects and they now have fish ponds. One man is anxious to get some assistance because he wants to build a small power plant. Would that be too small?

speakerposition: Minister of Resources and Development
subtopic: ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES FOR CONSERVATION PURPOSES
speechtext:
Each project would have to be reviewed on its merits. Whether or not it was too small or too large would depend upon the size of the project, the revenues of the province, and the willingness of the municipality and the provincial government to participate and bring it forward for consideration. Each project would have to be considered on its own merits.
[Mr. Browne (St. John's West).!

subtopic: ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES FOR CONSERVATION PURPOSES
speechtext: Suppose a province refuses to call for tenders. What happens?

speakerposition: Minister of Resources and Development
subtopic: ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES FOR CONSERVATION PURPOSES
speechtext: It is part of the practice in federal government operations of this kind to let contracts on the basis of tender, and it would be the intention under the bill to have that practice followed.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES FOR CONSERVATION PURPOSES
speechtext: Suppose the authority in the province does not want to agree to the calling of tenders?

speakerposition: Minister of Resources and Development
subtopic: ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES FOR CONSERVATION PURPOSES
speechtext: We would then have to decide whether or not there would be an agreement under the act. We are not committed to an agreement. If conditions are not such as to conform with the terms of the practice people would normally expect of us we would not enter into an agreement.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES FOR CONSERVATION PURPOSES
speechtext: Then the same thing would happen as happened with the highway program.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES FOR CONSERVATION PURPOSES
speechtext: Do you want me to call it six o'clock?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES FOR CONSERVATION PURPOSES
speechtext: There are only a few sections of the bill left. I cannot recall how many speeches were made, but we had quite a discussion at the resolution stage, and we have spent some time on second reading this afternoon. There are only four or five sections left, and perhaps the house would bear with us for a few minutes.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES FOR CONSERVATION PURPOSES
speechtext: Six o'clock.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES FOR CONSERVATION PURPOSES
speechtext:
I think we might pay some heed to the melodious voice of the Minister of Public Works and carry on a little longer by common consent. Personally I do not like to see a tendency on the part of the house or the chairman of the committee to force any legislation through. The minister has told us that this special legislation was designed in order to enlist the interest and co-operation of the provinces. I would ask him if he or his department have received any direct communications from provinces other than Ontario. Have any been received from the province of Nova Scotia or the province of Saskatchewan? Since the legislation was before the house at the resolution stage there has been very heavy flooding in the province of Nova Scotia. Considerable damage was done in certain places, in Oxford in my county and in Truro in Colchester county, as well as in other parts of Nova Scotia.
I would ask the minister if any communications have been received from the province of Nova Scotia and whether he has

made any direct representations to them. I would also ask whether there have been any similar contacts with the province of Saskatchewan. When this legislation was in the resolution stage discussions were held in connection with the South Saskatchewan dam, irrigation and control of flooding in the province of Saskatchewan. I would like to have a statement from the minister.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES FOR CONSERVATION PURPOSES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think this is too important a measure to be shoved through the house under pressure. We may be desirous of getting away from here by a certain date, but the time to have begun to prepare for that was several weeks ago, not when we have a measure of this kind before us. We have an hour for adjourning, and I think we should adhere to it.
